newsitem.title: JAMAICA: Caribbean nations discuss trade at Jamaica summit.
newsitem.headline: Caribbean nations discuss trade at Jamaica summit.

text.p: Heads of government of the 14-member Caribbean Community (Caricom) went into their first day of discussions on Tuesday to hammer out mechanisms for boosting trade with the rest of the world.
Jamaica's Prime Minister and Caricom Chairman P.J. Patterson said at Monday evening's opening ceremony that the task facing the region was an arduous one.
"We are about to embark on the most far-reaching cluster of trade and economic cooperation arrangements in which our nations have ever been engaged," he said.
The leaders aimed to develop a Regional Negotiating Mechanism (RNM) to handle virtually all of the myriad trade deliberations Caricom will enter into over the next several years.

These include the Free Trade Agreement of the Americas, the renewal of the Lome trade-and-aid convention with the European Union, an appeal of the World Trade Organisation's ruling against the EU's preferential banana import regime, and trade accords to be negotiated with Central America, the Dominican Republic, and the Andean Pact and Mercosur trade groups.
Discussions with the Central American Common Market, the Dominican Republic and the Andean Pact will likely start at the end of this month, according to a senior Caricom official.

Talks with Mercosur, grouping southern Latin American nations, will initially focus on mutual cooperation, but Jamaica's junior foreign minister Anthony Hylton said substantial deepening of ties is expected "within the next year."

President Lionel Fernandez of the Dominican Republic and Rene Preval of Haiti were expected to join the summit Thursday, when EU Commissioner for Development Joao Pinheiro will join the leaders for what is being called "an exchange of views" on both Lome and the banana issue.
Zimbabwean trade minister Nathan Shamuyaira will also join those talks, following the visit by a Caricom delegation to the recent Organisation of African Unity summit.

Europe is also proposing to expand Lome into a two-way free trade accord, something which the region's chief trade negotiator, former Commonwealth secretary-general Sir Shridath Ramphal, said must be approached with extreme caution.
"The issue of reciprocity must...face the question of the added burdens it would impose on already fragile manufacturing sectors from increased EU competition," he said.

Referring to the WTO ruling earlier this year, which found that part of the EU banana import regime violates WTO rules, Ramphal said that as part of the multitude of trade talks the Caribbean "will have to be vigilant that the WTO remains faithful to its mission."

"If it drifts into becoming a 'rich country club' protecting the interests only of the strong, a trade version of the International Monetary Fund, its moral authority will be lost and its mandate will be revisited," he added.
The region is insisting that it be given a longer period of adjustment when the planned Free Trade Agreement of the Americas comes into force in 2005.
